topics.title: Stem-and-leaf plots and back-to-back stem-and-leaf plots

questions.stem:
The monthly car sales for 16 dealerships are shown below. Make an ordered stem-and-leaf plot.
\[ 56, 39, 48, 65, 42, 59, 37, 49, 50, 44, 38, 58, 40, 59, 39, 47 \]
questions.answer: Sample answer: use the ordered stem-and-leaf plot shown. Key: 3 | 7 = 37 cars. The leaves are ordered within each stem.
questions.hint: Sort the values first, then use the tens digits as stems and list the units digits as ordered leaves.

keyPoints.note: There should be one leaf for every data value.
Keep each row of leaves in ascending order.

steps.explain: Order all 16 sales values from least to greatest before separating tens and units.
Use each tens digit as a stem and order the units digits as leaves.
Check that each leaf represents one original value and that there are 16 leaves.

questions.stem: The marks of 10 students on an examination are shown in the stem-and-leaf plot below (key: $5|7 = 57$). What is the mean examination mark for these students?

steps.explain: Read off every individual mark from the stem-and-leaf plot (stem = tens digit, leaf = units digit), in order.
Add all ten marks together to find the total.
The mean is the sum divided by the number of data values ($n=10$).

questions.stem: Find the median of the data presented in the dot plot below.

steps.explain: Find the total number of data points by adding up every score's frequency (dot count).
List every value in ascending order using the given frequencies: one $1$, three $2$s, two $3$s, one $4$, one $6$.
Since $n=8$ is even, the median is the average of the $\frac{n}{2}$th and $\left(\frac{n}{2}+1\right)$th values — i.e. the 4th and 5th values in the ordered list.
Average these two middle values to find the median.

questions.stem: Using the 16 dealership sales data, what is the median number of cars sold?
questions.hint: Read the data in order and average the two middle values because there are 16 values.

keyPoints.note: With an even number of data values, average the two central values.
First order the data, then locate positions 8 and 9.

steps.explain: There are 16 observations, so the median is the mean of positions 8 and 9.
The 8th and 9th ordered values are 47 and 48.
The median is 47.5 cars.

questions.stem: For the data set 29, 24, 30, 11, 32, 29, 24, 26, 25, 28, 29, find the median.
questions.hint: Order the 11 values; with an odd count, the median is the 6th value.

keyPoints.note: Sort all observations before finding the middle value.

steps.explain: Order the values from least to greatest.
There are 11 values, so select position 6.
The 6th value is 28.

questions.stem: For the data set 29, 24, 30, 11, 32, 29, 24, 26, 25, 28, 29, find the mean.
questions.hint: Add the values, then divide by the number of values.

keyPoints.note: The mean uses every data value: sum ÷ count.

steps.explain: Add all 11 observations.
Divide the total by 11.
To 2 decimal places, the mean is 26.09.

questions.stem: Given the following frequency distribution. Find correct to 2 decimal places the mean
questions.hint: Mean \(=\dfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f}\): multiply each score by its frequency, add these products, and divide by the total frequency.

keyPoints.note: A frequency table lists each score once with how many times it occurs — 4 students scored 20, 12 scored 30, and so on.
Divide by the number of SCORES (total frequency 50), not by the number of rows (6).

steps.explain: Find the total frequency (how many scores there are altogether).
Multiply each score by its frequency (the \(fx\) column).
Add the \(fx\) column.
Divide the sum of the scores by the total frequency.
Write the answer to 2 decimal places.
Common error: averaging the six score values \(\tfrac{20+30+40+50+60+70}{6}=45\) ignores the frequencies.

questions.stem: Given the following frequency distribution. Find correct to 2 decimal places the median
questions.hint: There are 50 scores, so the median is the average of the 25th and 26th scores. Build a cumulative frequency column to see which score each position falls in.

keyPoints.note: A frequency table lists each score once with how many times it occurs — 4 students scored 20, 12 scored 30, and so on.
Even number of scores (50): median = average of the 25th and 26th scores.

steps.explain: Total frequency (from the table).
With an even number of scores, the median is midway between the two middle positions.
Build the cumulative frequency (running total) for each score.
Scores in positions 1–4 are 20, positions 5–16 are 30, positions 17–34 are 40. Both the 25th and 26th positions lie in 17–34.
Average the two middle scores.

questions.stem: Given the following frequency distribution. Find correct to 2 decimal places the mode
questions.hint: The mode is the SCORE with the highest frequency — read across from the biggest number in the Frequency column.

keyPoints.note: A frequency table lists each score once with how many times it occurs — 4 students scored 20, 12 scored 30, and so on.
The answer is a score (20, 30, 40, …), not the frequency itself.

steps.explain: Look down the Frequency column for the largest value.
Read across to find which score has that frequency.
The mode is the score that occurs most often.
Common error: answering 18 (the frequency) or 70 (the largest score).

questions.stem: Given the following frequency distribution. Find correct to 2 decimal places the interquartile range
questions.hint: Split the 50 scores into a lower half (positions 1–25) and upper half (26–50). \(Q_1\) is the median of the lower half (13th score), \(Q_3\) the median of the upper half (38th score). IQR \(=Q_3-Q_1\).

keyPoints.note: A frequency table lists each score once with how many times it occurs — 4 students scored 20, 12 scored 30, and so on.
IQR = upper quartile − lower quartile; it measures the spread of the middle 50% of scores.

steps.explain: Cumulative frequencies (running totals).
Lower half = positions 1 to 25. Its median is the 13th score.
Positions 5–16 are all 30, so the 13th score is 30.
Upper half = positions 26 to 50 (25 scores). Its median is the 13th of those, i.e. position \(25+13=38\).
Positions 35–48 are all 50, so the 38th score is 50.
Subtract.
Common error: the RANGE is \(70-20=50\); the IQR ignores the extreme quarter of scores at each end.

questions.hint: The mode is the value that occurs most often. Count the frequency of each value.

keyPoints.note: Choose the value that appears most often.

steps.explain: Count the repeated values in the data set. The value 2 appears three times; each other value appears once.
Select the value with the greatest frequency.

questions.stem: What is the median of the following data set? \(11,14,23,28,32,40\).
questions.hint: There are 6 values, so the median is the average of the 3rd and 4th values after ordering.

keyPoints.note: For an even number of values, average the two central values.

steps.explain: The data are already in ascending order. Since there are 6 values, there are two middle values.
Average the 3rd and 4th values.

questions.hint: For part (a), use IQR = Q3 − Q1. For part (b), compare the new longest time with the original Q3 boundary.

keyPoints.note: The right edge of the box is Q3 and the left edge is Q1.

parts.stem: After the students completed the training camp. It is found that the longest time taken by the students to finish a 100 m race is 2.9 seconds less than the time taken before the camp. The trainer claims that at least 25% of the students showed improvement after the camp. Do you agree? Justify your answer with the appropriate mathematical reasoning.
parts.answer: Yes. The longest time after camp is \(18.1-2.9=15.2\) seconds, below the original upper quartile \(15.3\) seconds. Therefore the students who were at or above that original upper-quartile boundary (at least the slowest 25%) must have improved.
parts.hint: Compare the new maximum time with the original third quartile. The upper quartile marks the slowest quarter boundary.

keyPoints.note: Compare the new maximum with the original third quartile.

steps.explain: From part (a), the original upper quartile is 15.3 seconds. The original longest time is 18.1 seconds.
